title: Building the Company: A System That Works When You Are Not in the Room
summary: A development company is not its founder; it is the set of decisions, people, records and controls that keep working when the founder is absent. This lesson frames the board, delegation of authority, the order of hiring, key-person risk, operating systems and personal brand as one design problem.
body:
A company exists to make good decisions repeatable without you. If every important decision still needs your presence, you have built a job, not a company, and a lender, an investor and your heirs will all price it that way.

Recall

Q. What is return on equity in place?

A. Annual cash flow after debt service and reserves divided by the equity you could take out of the building today, after debt, selling costs and, for comparison, tax.

Q. What is the difference between property management and asset management?

A. Property management runs the building day to day. Asset management owns the business plan: budget, rent strategy, capital, financing and exit.

Q. When reverse engineering a finished building, why study its sequence and logistics and not only its cost?

A. Because how a building was built, cycle times, crane and hoist plans, and the order of trades, explains its cost and schedule, and that is the part a developer can actually copy.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, the move from one project to several is where many capable developers stall. On one project, your judgement is the system: you read every invoice, attend every meeting, and remember every promise. On three projects, that same habit becomes the bottleneck, and the risk that matters most is no longer the market or the ground. It is you: your time, your health, your absence. Kema joins me this week because building a company is as much about how you work as about legal structure.

Governance is the decision map

In plain English: governance answers who decides what, on what information, and who checks it afterwards.

The professional framing has three layers. Owners, the shareholders or members, decide the few things only owners should decide: who sits on the board, major structural changes, selling the company. The board of directors sets strategy, approves major commitments, appoints and oversees management, and holds the duties the law places on directors. Management runs the business within limits the board sets. In a small company, you may sit in all three layers at once. That is legal and common. The discipline is to know which hat you are wearing when you sign, because the law and your investors will ask.

Many founders add an advisory board first: experienced people who give advice but hold no legal authority and carry no directors' duties. It is a sensible step, provided nobody, including you, confuses advice with oversight. A board with at least one genuinely independent director, someone with no financial tie to you or the company, is the next step, and it is the one lenders and institutional investors notice.

The delegation of authority

In plain English: write down who can approve what, up to what amount, so that decisions do not wait for you and do not happen without anyone.

A delegation of authority matrix lists each decision type down the side, such as signing a contract, approving a change order, approving a draw, hiring, paying an invoice or committing to a site, and for each it states who may approve, up to what limit, and who must be told. A worked example with hypothetical round numbers: a project manager may approve change orders up to 25,000 dollars within contingency; the chief executive up to 250,000 dollars; above that, the board. Any change that moves the completion date or uses more than half of remaining contingency goes to the chief executive regardless of amount. The numbers are your choice, not a standard. What matters is that they exist, that they are written, and that the bank's signing mandate matches them.

Say that out loud now.

If the delegation is not written, every decision either waits for me or happens without anyone.

Key-person risk and the order of hiring

Key-person risk is the risk that the company's value or obligations depend on one person who could leave, fall ill or die. For a young developer, that person is usually the founder. Lenders see it in guarantees, investors in the management clause, and partners in the agreements that let them remove you or buy you out. The controls are four: documented processes, so that knowledge lives in records rather than in one head; a named deputy for each critical role; insurance concepts such as key-person cover, which a licensed adviser must assess; and legal arrangements, including powers of attorney and a shareholders' agreement that says what happens on death or disability.

The order of hiring follows the risk. The first hire for most developers is not a second dealmaker; it is someone who keeps the money honest, a controller or project accountant who runs the monthly close, reconciles bank accounts and prepares draw packages. The second is someone who controls delivery, an owner's project manager. Deal finding stays with the founder longest, because it is the hardest to delegate and the most personal. A second worked example: if you can afford two hires at a hypothetical 120,000 dollars each fully loaded, a controller and a project manager free perhaps half your week; a second dealmaker frees none of it and doubles the number of commitments you must oversee.

Systems, and the brand they build

The systems that matter in a small development company are few: a document control system with one current version of every contract and drawing; a monthly close that produces project cost reports and company accounts on a fixed day; an approval workflow that enforces the delegation matrix; a decision log; and a compliance calendar. None needs expensive software. All need an owner and a date.

Personal brand belongs here, not in marketing. Your reputation with lenders, consultants and authorities is the sum of what the systems produce: reports on time, numbers that reconcile, promises kept by Friday. A strong personal brand is a by-product of a company that behaves predictably, and it transfers to the company only if the company keeps behaving that way when you are not in the room.

How the best do it

Well-run development and construction firms tend to separate the people who originate deals from the people who approve them, usually through an investment committee with written criteria, and they keep a delegation of authority that every bank mandate and every contract signature must match. A small developer can copy both on day one: a two-person investment committee that includes one outsider, and a one-page delegation matrix.

Six-Lens Check

Tax: how employees, contractors and fees are treated for tax depends on local rules; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it. Liability: directors carry personal duties, and a clear delegation shows they were exercised. Banking: signing mandates must match the delegation matrix. Governance: one independent voice, written approval limits and a decision log. Estate: a shareholders' agreement and powers of attorney decide what happens to the company if you cannot act. Exit: a company that depends on its founder is worth little to a buyer or successor.

Professional sign-off required: lawyer, on the shareholders' agreement and board structure; licensed insurance adviser, on key-person cover.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a company in which every critical decision, record and relationship sits with the founder, so that one illness halts everything and no one else can prove what was agreed. The control is a written delegation matrix, documented processes with named deputies, and legal arrangements for incapacity.

The beginner's mistake

Hiring a second dealmaker before a controller. More deals with the same weak controls multiply the risk, not the company.

Callback

In Week 48, Marco taught the project charter, governance and the owner decision log. That was governance for one project. This week the same tools scale to the company: the charter becomes the strategy, the project decision log becomes the board's minutes, and approval authorities become the delegation matrix.

Recap

A company is a system that makes good decisions repeatable without the founder. Governance assigns decisions to owners, the board and management. A written delegation matrix sets limits. Key-person risk is reduced through process, deputies, insurance concepts and legal arrangements. Hire controls before more deals. Brand is what your systems produce.

Next: Ford, with Cole, on Failure Forensics: WeWork in 2019, and governance built around one person.
checklist: I can name which hat I wear, owner, director or manager, when I sign each document.
I have a written delegation of authority with approval limits for each decision type.
My bank signing mandates match the delegation matrix.
I have at least one independent voice reviewing major commitments.
Each critical role has a named deputy and documented processes.
My first hires strengthen controls before they add deal volume.
I have a shareholders' agreement and powers of attorney that cover incapacity.
I run a monthly close on a fixed day.
head: Field checklist
speak: A company exists to make good decisions repeatable without me. Governance answers who decides what, on what information, and who checks it. Owners appoint the board and decide structural matters. The board sets strategy, approves major commitments and oversees management. Management runs the business within limits. I may hold all three roles, so I must know which hat I wear when I sign. The core tool is a written delegation of authority: each decision type, who may approve it, up to what amount, and who must be told, matched to the bank's signing mandate. Key-person risk, usually me, is reduced by documented processes, named deputies, insurance concepts assessed by a licensed adviser, and a shareholders' agreement and powers of attorney for incapacity. I hire a controller before a second dealmaker, because more deals with weak controls multiply risk. And my personal brand is simply what these systems produce, every month.
terms: Delegation of authority — a written schedule of who may approve each type of decision, up to what limit, and who must be informed.
Key-person risk — the risk that a company's value or obligations depend on one individual who could leave, fall ill or die.
Independent director — a director with no financial or family tie to management or controlling owners, able to judge their proposals objectively.

hostile.q: If you were incapacitated tomorrow, who signs the next draw certificate, and how would I know they have the authority?
hostile.a: The delegation of authority names our controller and project director as joint signatories for draw certificates up to the approved budget, and the board resolution that grants it is in your file with their specimen signatures. Above that, an independent director countersigns. My powers of attorney and the shareholders' agreement cover my own position. I can send you all four documents today.

title: WeWork, 2019: Governance Built Around One Person
summary: In August 2019 WeWork's parent made public an offering document that revealed founder control through special voting shares and a series of dealings between the company and its founder. Investors balked, the founder stepped down as chief executive in September and the offering was withdrawn at the end of that month. Cole assists on governance and related-party dealing in seven forensic steps.
body:
WeWork did not fail in 2019 because its buildings were bad. Its planned public offering collapsed when the documents showed that one person controlled the company and also did business with it, and that the structure gave outsiders little power to check either.

Recall

Q. What is a delegation of authority?

A. A written schedule of who may approve each type of decision, up to what limit, and who must be informed.

Q. In a hold, sell or refinance decision, why compare options at the same future date?

A. Because cash today and wealth later are not comparable unless released cash is grown at the same after-tax alternative return to one date.

Q. What does reverse engineering a finished building teach a developer?

A. How its structure, systems, sequence and logistics explain its cost and schedule, which tells you what to copy and what to avoid.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Cole joins me because this case is about governance and related-party dealing, which is his field. It also concerns real estate: WeWork leased large amounts of office space and re-let it as flexible workspace. The lesson for a small developer is not about scale or technology narratives. It is about what happens when the founder is the controlling owner, the chief executive and a counterparty all at once.

I will state only what was widely documented: the public filing in August 2019, its disclosures in general terms, the founder's resignation as chief executive in September, the withdrawal of the offering on 30 September 2019, and the later Chapter 11 filing in November 2023. Where I describe dynamics, I describe them generally, without figures.

1. Timeline

WeWork grew rapidly through the 2010s, funded by large private investment, signing long leases and offering short-term memberships. In August 2019 its parent, then called The We Company, made public its registration statement for an initial public offering, the document that must disclose risks, governance and related-party transactions. Analysts and investors focused on the governance disclosures, the scale of losses and the long lease obligations. In September 2019 the offering was postponed, and on 24 September the co-founder, Adam Neumann, stepped down as chief executive. On 30 September 2019 the company withdrew its registration. Its largest investor, SoftBank, then led a rescue. The company later went public by another route in 2021 and filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in the United States in November 2023.

2. Key decisions

Three governance decisions mattered. Creating share classes that gave the founder voting control far beyond his economic ownership. Allowing transactions between the company and its founder, including leases of buildings in which he held interests, loans, and a payment to him for rights to the "We" name, later reversed. And keeping a board whose independence from the founder outsiders doubted.

3. Assumptions

The assumptions were that public investors would accept founder control as private investors had, that rapid growth would justify losses and lease commitments, and that related-party dealings would be read as alignment rather than conflict. The first assumption failed the moment the disclosures were read by people with no prior commitment to the story.

4. Incentives

Private investors who had valued the company highly had an incentive to support a public valuation that confirmed their own. Advisers earned fees for completing the offering. The founder held control and therefore had little structural reason to give it up. Growth was rewarded over profit. None of those incentives favoured an independent check.

Say that out loud now.

When the same person controls the company and does business with it, the only protection is a check that person does not control.

5. Warning signs ignored

Related-party leases and loans had been reported in the press before the filing. Losses were large and rising with growth. Long lease obligations sat against short member commitments, a maturity mismatch in operating form. Each signal was visible to insiders long before the public document made it impossible to ignore.

6. Point of no return

For the 2019 offering, the point of no return came when the disclosures reached the public market. Governance that might have been negotiated privately was now judged by investors with alternatives and no sunk commitment, and the founder's departure followed within weeks.

7. Root cause

The root cause was governance designed around one person rather than around checks on that person: control without accountability, and conflicts without independent approval. The business model's risks were real, but the governance determined that nobody with power was positioned to slow them.

Cole's view: the related-party test

Cole here. In a small development company, related-party dealing is common and often harmless: the founder leases a site he owns to a project company, lends it money, or charges a fee through another entity. The test is not whether it happens, but how it is approved. Three questions. Was it disclosed in writing to everyone whose money is affected? Was it approved by someone with no interest in it, such as an independent director or the investors themselves? And is the price supported by evidence of a market rate, such as an independent appraisal or competing quotes?

A worked example with hypothetical round numbers. You own a site through a personal company and want to sell it to a development partnership in which outside investors hold 70 percent. You propose a price of 4,000,000 dollars. Two independent appraisals say 3,600,000 and 3,800,000 dollars. A clean process discloses your interest, provides both appraisals, sets the price at or below their average, 3,700,000 dollars, and obtains written approval from the investors or an independent director. A failed process sets 4,000,000 dollars, discloses it in a footnote and asks investors to trust you. The difference of 300,000 dollars is small. The difference in trust is not.

What a small developer copies

Three habits come out of this case. First, keep a related-party register: a single list of every arrangement between you, your family or your other entities and any company or project you manage, with the date it was disclosed, who approved it and the evidence of price. Update it before any new arrangement is signed, not after. Second, match control with accountability. If you hold voting control, offset it with written limits on what you may approve alone, and give an independent director or the investors a veto on conflicts. Third, read your own governance documents once a year as an outside investor with alternatives would, the way public investors read WeWork's filing in 2019. Ask which disclosure would make you hesitate if someone else had written it.

None of this slows a good deal. A conflict approved through a clean process closes on time and stays closed. One approved on trust is reopened by the first investor who reads the footnote, often at the worst moment, such as a refinance or a sale.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a founder who holds control and also transacts with the company, with no independent approval of the conflicts. The control is written disclosure of every related-party arrangement, approval by someone without an interest, and price evidence from an independent source.

The beginner's mistake

Believing that because a related-party deal is fair, it does not need a process. Investors cannot see fairness; they can only see process.

Callback

In Week 75, Ford and Cole ran the second post-mortem: governance capture, related-party dealing and handshake deals. WeWork is that lesson at public-market scale. The mechanism is identical in a two-building company: the conflict is not the failure; the missing check is.

Recap

In August 2019 WeWork's public filing showed founder voting control, transactions between the company and its founder, and doubts about board independence. Investors balked, the founder stepped down as chief executive on 24 September, and the offering was withdrawn on 30 September 2019. The company filed for Chapter 11 in November 2023.

Rule 128: Never transact with your own company without written disclosure, independent approval and independent price evidence; the more control you hold, the stronger the check you must build on yourself.

Next: Nadia on The Money: what a development company costs to run, and which fees pay for it.
checklist: I disclose every related-party arrangement in writing to everyone whose money it affects.
I obtain approval of conflicts from someone with no interest in them.
I support related-party prices with independent appraisals or quotes.
I keep voting control proportionate to accountability, not only to ambition.
I appoint at least one director outsiders would accept as independent.
I read my own governance as an outside investor with alternatives would.
I treat a press report of a conflict as a warning, not noise.
head: Field checklist
speak: In August 2019, WeWork's parent made public the document for its initial public offering. It showed that the co-founder, Adam Neumann, held voting control through special share classes far beyond his economic stake, and that the company had dealt with him directly, including leases of buildings he had interests in, loans, and a payment for the We name that was later reversed. Investors with alternatives balked. The offering was postponed, he stepped down as chief executive on 24 September 2019, and the offering was withdrawn on 30 September. SoftBank led a rescue, and the company filed for Chapter 11 in November 2023. The root cause was governance built around one person instead of around checks on that person. Rule 128: never transact with my own company without written disclosure, independent approval and independent price evidence, and the more control I hold, the stronger the check I build on myself.
terms: Related-party transaction — a deal between a company and a person or entity connected to its controllers, such as a founder, director or their affiliates.
Multi-class shares — share classes with different voting rights, which can give one holder control beyond their economic ownership.
Registration statement — the offering document filed with a securities regulator before a public offering, disclosing risks, governance and related-party dealings.

hostile.q: Your company is buying the site from you personally. Why should the investors believe the price?
hostile.a: They should not have to believe me. They have two independent appraisals, my interest disclosed in writing, and a price set at the average of the two, not my asking figure. The decision is theirs, by written approval, or the independent director's if they prefer. If either appraisal is challenged, I will commission a third from a firm they choose, at the partnership's cost.

rule: Rule 128: Never transact with your own company without written disclosure, independent approval and independent price evidence; the more control you hold, the stronger the check you must build on yourself.

title: What a Development Company Costs, and Which Fees Pay for It
summary: A development company has two kinds of money: project money that belongs to each partnership, and company money that pays the team between and across deals. This lesson builds a company overhead budget, matches it to fee streams, prices a hire and the company's runway, and closes with Warrick's Wealth Ledger.
body:
Project profit arrives years apart; payroll arrives every two weeks. A development company survives on the gap between those two calendars, so the first financial skill is to know exactly what the company costs and which steady fees cover it.

Recall

Q. What is the related-party test Cole taught?

A. Written disclosure to everyone affected, approval by someone with no interest, and price evidence from an independent source.

Q. When does a cash-out refinance pay?

A. When the cash released earns more than the cash flow given up divided by the cash taken out, and the building can carry the higher debt service through a fall in NOI.

Q. In a reverse-engineered building, what does cost per square metre on its own fail to tell you?

A. Why the cost was what it was: the structure, systems, sequence and logistics behind it, which are the parts that can be copied or avoided.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, many developers measure success project by project and discover that the company itself is quietly losing money. The projects make profits on paper, the promotes arrive after exit, and in between the company pays salaries, rent, insurance and advisers from whatever it can find. That gap pushes owners into bad deals simply to earn a fee. This lesson separates the two kinds of money and shows how to fund the company honestly. All numbers are hypothetical round figures.

Two pockets: project money and company money

In plain English: money raised for a building belongs to that building's owners. The company that manages it is paid separately, through fees agreed in the documents.

The professional framing: each project usually sits in its own entity, with its own bank account, its own budget and its own investors. The development company, the sponsor, earns fees from each project for the services it provides, and may earn a promote, a share of profit above investors' return hurdles, at the end. Company overhead, which is salaries, office, insurance, systems and professional fees not charged to any one project, must be paid from those fees. Paying company costs from project accounts without authority in the documents is a breach and, in some circumstances, worse. Keep the pockets separate.

The company overhead budget

A worked example. A small development company has four people: the founder, a controller, a project manager and an analyst. Fully loaded cost, meaning salary plus benefits, payroll costs and equipment, is a hypothetical 150,000, 120,000, 130,000 and 90,000 dollars, totalling 490,000 dollars. Office and systems cost 60,000 dollars. Insurance, including directors and officers cover and professional liability, costs 40,000 dollars. Legal, accounting and audit for the company itself cost 60,000 dollars. Travel and business development cost 50,000 dollars. Total annual overhead: 700,000 dollars, or about 58,300 dollars a month.

That monthly figure is the most important number in the company. Every decision to hire, lease an office or pursue a deal should be measured against it.

Which fees pay for it

Common sponsor fees, all set by commercial practice and negotiated deal by deal, include a development fee, often expressed as a percentage of project costs and paid over the development period; an asset management fee, often a percentage of revenue or of equity, paid during operations; sometimes a construction management or oversight fee; and transaction fees at acquisition, financing or sale. The promote comes last and is uncertain.

Continue the example. One project has a hypothetical total cost of 30,000,000 dollars and pays a development fee of 3 percent, 900,000 dollars, spread over a 36-month development period: 25,000 dollars a month. Two stabilised buildings pay asset management fees totalling 15,000 dollars a month. Company fee income is 40,000 dollars a month against overhead of 58,300 dollars. The company is short 18,300 dollars a month, about 220,000 dollars a year, which the founder is funding from personal savings while waiting for a promote.

Say that out loud now.

Steady fees must cover steady costs. The promote is a reward, not a salary.

The runway and the cost of a hire

A company's runway is the number of months its cash can cover the shortfall between overhead and fee income. If the company holds 440,000 dollars and the monthly shortfall is 18,300 dollars, the runway is about 24 months. This is the same countdown Roman taught for reserves, applied to the company itself.

Now price a hire. A second project manager costs 130,000 dollars a year fully loaded, about 10,800 dollars a month. Hired today with no new fee income, the shortfall rises to 29,100 dollars a month and the runway falls to about 15 months. The hire pays only if it brings in, or protects, more than 10,800 dollars a month: for example by enabling a second project whose development fee is 25,000 dollars a month. Write the hire's business case in those terms before signing the offer letter.

Closing the gap honestly

There are only four honest ways to close the overhead gap in the example. Raise recurring fee income, by managing more buildings, including buildings owned by others. Time development fees better, for example negotiating a larger share at financing close rather than evenly over the build, which is a commercial term the investors must accept. Reduce overhead, starting with costs that do not create fees. Or fund the gap deliberately with company equity, sized to the runway, rather than by drift. Two dishonest ways also exist: charging the company's costs to projects without authority, and pursuing a weak deal for its fee. A written overhead budget makes the dishonest ways visible before they start.

A small example of timing. If the 900,000 dollar development fee were paid one third at financing close and two thirds over the build, the company would receive 300,000 dollars up front and then about 16,700 dollars a month. The total is the same; the runway is not. Investors will often accept some front-loading if the fee is tied to milestones, such as financing close and substantial completion, rather than to the calendar.

What the company is worth

A development company is usually valued, if at all, on the reliability of its fee streams and the transferability of its relationships, not on project profits that belong to investors. A company whose fees depend on the founder's personal involvement is worth much less to a buyer or a successor. Recurring asset management fees from long-held buildings are generally valued more highly than one-off development fees. The methods and multiples are market practice and vary; describe value in terms of what recurs and what would survive the founder's absence.

Warrick's Wealth Ledger

Warrick here. On your personal balance sheet, the company appears twice. Once as an asset, your shares, which are illiquid and hard to value. Once as a hidden liability, if you are funding its overhead shortfall or have guaranteed its office lease or credit line. Record the monthly subsidy you provide as a real outflow, and count your guarantees as contingent liabilities. Most important, recognise that your own working life, your human capital, is the company's largest asset, which is why key-person cover and disability concepts belong on the ledger. A licensed adviser is required before you act.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is funding overhead from hope, the expected promote, until the founder takes a poor deal for its fee or borrows from project accounts. The control is an overhead budget matched to recurring fees, a monthly runway report, and a rule that every hire has a fee-based business case.

The beginner's mistake

Counting the promote as company income before it is earned. It arrives late, if at all, and it depends on investors receiving their return first.

Callback

In Week 38, JAX and Elias taught waterfalls: preferred return, catch-up, promote, clawback and developer fees and their tax character. That lesson was about who gets paid on a project. This one is about whether the company that runs the projects can survive until it does.

Recap

Keep project money and company money separate. Build an overhead budget and a monthly figure. Match it to recurring fees, not the promote. Report runway monthly. Price each hire against the fee income it creates or protects. Value the company on what recurs without you.

Next: Omar on The Rules: directors' duties, conflicts, shareholders' agreements and the law of employing people.
checklist: I keep project bank accounts and company accounts completely separate.
I know my monthly company overhead to the nearest thousand dollars.
I match overhead to recurring fees, not to expected promotes.
I report the company's runway in months every month.
I write a fee-based business case before any hire.
I record any personal subsidy of the company as a real outflow.
I list every guarantee I give the company as a contingent liability.
head: Field checklist
speak: A development company has two pockets. Project money belongs to each project's investors. Company money comes from fees the documents allow: development fees during construction, asset management fees during operations, sometimes transaction fees, and a promote at the end that is uncertain. In my hypothetical example, four people, an office, insurance and advisers cost 700,000 dollars a year, about 58,300 a month. A development fee of 25,000 a month and asset management fees of 15,000 a month leave a 18,300 dollar monthly shortfall. With 440,000 dollars in the bank, the runway is about 24 months. A second project manager at 10,800 a month cuts that to about 15 months unless he brings in more fee income than he costs. So steady fees must cover steady costs, the promote is a reward not a salary, and every hire needs a fee-based business case. A company is worth what recurs without me.
terms: Sponsor — the company that organises, manages and usually invests alongside investors in a real estate project.
Company overhead — costs of running the development company itself that are not charged to any one project, such as salaries, office and insurance.
Company runway — the number of months company cash can cover the shortfall between overhead and recurring fee income.

hostile.q: Your company's overhead exceeds its fees. How do I know you won't pay it from my project's account?
hostile.a: Because the documents do not allow it and the controls prevent it. Each project has its own account with dual signatories, and any payment to the sponsor must match a fee schedule approved in the agreement. You receive the monthly bank reconciliation. The company's shortfall is funded from its own capital, which shows on its accounts with a runway report I will send you each quarter.

title: The Rules of the Company: Directors' Duties, Conflicts and the Agreements That Outlive You
summary: Company law places duties on directors, sets rules for conflicts of interest, and leaves much of the rest to the shareholders' agreement. Employment law decides who is an employee. This lesson teaches the concepts so that you know which documents to build and which professional to engage.
body:
Company law gives directors duties that cannot simply be signed away, and gives owners the freedom to write most of the rest into a shareholders' agreement. A well-built company uses both: duties honoured in practice, and an agreement that settles the hard questions before anyone is angry.

Recall

Q. What is a company runway?

A. The number of months company cash can cover the shortfall between overhead and recurring fee income.

Q. What is realisation in tax?

A. The event, usually a sale or other disposition, that causes an increase in value to be measured and taxed.

Q. What is the multi-employer doctrine on construction sites?

A. A safety enforcement concept under which more than one employer on a site, such as a controlling contractor, can be responsible for a hazard that exposes another employer's workers. Verify its current application against the primary source.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, as your company grows, you will sign documents as a director, appoint others as directors, admit partners as shareholders and employ people. Each step creates legal relationships with their own rules. I teach concepts only. Company and employment law vary by jurisdiction and change. Verify every point against the primary source before you rely on it. Professional sign-off required: corporate lawyer and employment lawyer in each jurisdiction where you operate.

The duties of a director

In plain English: a director must act for the company, not for himself, and must take reasonable care.

The professional framing is two duties that appear in many common-law systems in some form. The duty of loyalty, often called the fiduciary duty, requires a director to act honestly and in good faith in the best interests of the company, to avoid conflicts between personal and company interests, and not to profit secretly from the position. The duty of care requires a director to exercise the care, diligence and skill that a reasonably prudent person would in comparable circumstances. To whom the duties are owed, and how far creditors and other stakeholders count when a company is near insolvency, varies by jurisdiction.

Many courts give directors latitude for honest business decisions made on reasonable information, often called the business judgment rule, a concept that protects the process of deciding more than the outcome. The practical lesson is that your protection is a record: papers circulated before the meeting, questions asked, advice obtained, and minutes that show the reasons. A director who approves a large commitment in a five-minute call with no papers is poorly protected whatever the result.

Conflicts of interest

Most company laws, and most well-drafted constitutions, require a director with a personal interest in a transaction to disclose it, and often to abstain from voting on it. Some transactions also need shareholder approval. Yesterday Cole showed the practical test; today the legal frame. A worked example with hypothetical round numbers: a director owns a firm bidding 400,000 dollars to provide services to the company. Under a typical rule, the director discloses the interest in writing, the disclosure is minuted, the director leaves the room, and the remaining directors decide on the evidence, such as competing bids of 380,000 and 430,000 dollars. If the board approves the director's firm despite a lower bid, the minutes should state the reason, for example a shorter programme with a quantified value.

Say that out loud now.

Disclose, leave the room, let others decide on evidence, and minute the reason.

The shareholders' agreement

A shareholders' agreement is a contract among the owners that covers what the law leaves to them. For a development company, the essential clauses are reserved matters, decisions needing a special majority or unanimous consent; board composition and appointment rights; transfer restrictions and rights of first refusal; tag-along and drag-along rights; deadlock resolution; and, above all, what happens on death, disability, departure or divorce.

The last group is where key-person risk becomes law. A buy-sell clause can require or allow the company or the other shareholders to buy a departing or deceased shareholder's shares at a price set by formula or valuation. Such a clause is only as good as its funding. A second worked example: the founder's shares are valued at a hypothetical 2,000,000 dollars. If the agreement obliges the other shareholders to buy them on death, they need 2,000,000 dollars on a date nobody can predict. Insurance on the founder's life, owned and paid as the agreement specifies, is one common way to fund it; the right structure needs a lawyer and a licensed adviser. Without funding, the clause can force a sale of the company's assets to pay the estate.

Employing people

Many systems distinguish employees from independent contractors, and the label in the contract does not decide it. Tests commonly look at control over how the work is done, integration into the business, who provides tools, the chance of profit or risk of loss, and exclusivity. Misclassifying an employee as a contractor can create liability for unpaid payroll taxes, benefits and penalties. Restraints such as non-compete clauses are enforced very differently across jurisdictions, and some places restrict them heavily. Confidentiality and ownership of work product, by contrast, are usually enforceable if drafted clearly.

A worked example of classification. A site supervisor works only for your company, full time, on your schedule, using your vehicle and tools, under your instructions on how the work is done, and is paid monthly regardless of results. Calling that person a contractor in the agreement does not make them one under most tests; the substance points to employment. By contrast, an independent cost consultant with several clients, her own firm, her own insurance and a fixed fee for a defined report looks like a contractor. When the facts fall between those poles, ask an employment lawyer before the first payment, not after a dispute.

Officers, signatures and the outside world

Directors decide as a board; officers, such as the chief executive or the controller, act for the company within authority the board gives them. Third parties such as banks and contractors usually rely on documents that show that authority: certified board resolutions, signing mandates and incumbency certificates naming the current officers. The delegation matrix you wrote on Day 1 must match those documents. When it does not, a counterparty may be entitled to rely on what it was shown, and the company may be bound by a signature its own rules did not allow.

Protecting the people who govern

Directors' and officers' liability insurance, often called D and O insurance, covers certain claims against directors and officers, subject to exclusions such as fraud. An indemnity in the company's constitution or a separate agreement can add protection, within what the law allows. An independent director will usually ask for both before joining, and is right to.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a company whose shareholders' agreement is silent or unfunded on death, disability and departure, so that the founder's absence triggers a dispute or a forced sale. The control is an agreement that addresses each event, with a valuation method and a funding source, reviewed whenever ownership or value changes.

The beginner's mistake

Thinking minutes are formalities. In a dispute, the minutes are the evidence of whether directors exercised care and handled conflicts properly.

Callback

In Week 21, LEX and Omar taught limited liability and piercing the corporate veil. That protection survives only if the company is treated as a separate person in practice. Directors' duties, minuted decisions and separate accounts are what keep the veil intact when a creditor tests it.

Recap

Directors owe duties of loyalty and care; their protection is a record of informed process. Conflicts need disclosure, abstention and evidence. The shareholders' agreement settles reserved matters, transfers, deadlock and the founder's absence, and a buy-sell clause needs funding. Employment status is decided by substance, not labels.

Next: Nadia on The Numbers: reverse engineering how many projects a company needs to pay for itself.
checklist: I know which decisions I make as director, and I keep a record of the information behind them.
Board papers are circulated before major decisions, and minutes record reasons.
Every director's conflict is disclosed in writing, minuted, and decided without that director.
Our shareholders' agreement covers death, disability, departure and divorce.
Every buy-sell obligation has a valuation method and a funding source.
I check employment status by substance, not by the contract label.
Directors have appropriate liability insurance and indemnities, reviewed by counsel.
head: Field checklist
speak: Directors owe two broad duties in many systems: loyalty, meaning acting honestly for the company and avoiding conflicts, and care, meaning the diligence a reasonably prudent person would show. Courts often protect honest decisions made on reasonable information, so my protection is a record: papers before the meeting, questions asked, advice taken, reasons minuted. A director with a conflict discloses it, leaves the room, and lets others decide on evidence. The shareholders' agreement settles what law leaves to owners: reserved matters, board seats, transfers, tag and drag, deadlock, and what happens on death, disability, departure or divorce. A buy-sell clause is only as good as its funding; without it, the founder's death can force a sale. Employment status depends on substance, not labels. And directors deserve proper insurance and indemnities. These are concepts; I verify each with corporate and employment lawyers in every jurisdiction.
terms: Duty of loyalty — a director's obligation to act honestly and in good faith in the company's best interests, avoiding conflicts and secret profit.
Duty of care — a director's obligation to exercise the care, diligence and skill a reasonably prudent person would in comparable circumstances.
Buy-sell clause — a provision in a shareholders' agreement requiring or allowing the purchase of a shareholder's interest on defined events, at a set price or by valuation.

hostile.q: Your shareholders' agreement obliges the others to buy your shares if you die. Where does the money come from?
hostile.a: From a funded source named in the agreement: insurance on my life, structured as the agreement specifies, sized to the current valuation method and reviewed annually as the company's value changes. The schedule showing the valuation, the cover and the review date is attached to the agreement. If cover were not available, the agreement allows payment over a set period from company cash flow, so the estate is paid without forcing an asset sale.

title: Reverse Engineering the Company: How Many Projects Pay for the Team?
summary: Start from the company you want, a team and an overhead budget with a safety margin, and work backward to the recurring fee income it needs, the projects and buildings that produce it, and the pipeline of opportunities required to win them. All numbers are hypothetical.
body:
Most founders ask how big their company can grow. The better question runs backward: what does the company I need cost, and how many projects, buildings and opportunities must exist to pay for it without depending on the promote?

Recall

Q. What is a buy-sell clause?

A. A provision in a shareholders' agreement requiring or allowing the purchase of a shareholder's interest on defined events, at a set price or by valuation, which needs a funding source to work.

Q. What is reinvestment risk?

A. The risk that money released by a sale cannot quickly be invested at a comparable return.

Q. What is the purpose of a capital needs assessment?

A. To list each building component, its remaining life and replacement cost, so a capital reserve can be sized against real replacement dates.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, the projects you pursue should follow from the company you need, not the other way round. When the arithmetic runs forward, from whatever deal appears, the company grows by accident and its overhead outruns its fees. When it runs backward, you know how many deals you need, of what size, and how wide the pipeline must be. All figures are hypothetical, and every fee level is commercial practice, negotiated deal by deal.

The finished outcome

Target: a company of five people, the founder, a controller, two project managers and an analyst, with overhead that is covered by recurring fees alone, plus a margin of safety of 20 percent. Overhead, built as Nadia did on Day 3, is 830,000 dollars a year: 620,000 dollars of people and 210,000 dollars of office, insurance, advisers and travel. With a 20 percent margin, the company needs about 1,000,000 dollars a year of fee income, roughly 83,300 dollars a month.

Step 1: split the target between fee types

Decide the mix. Development fees are larger but end when each project completes. Asset management fees are smaller but recur as long as you manage the buildings. A resilient company aims for recurring fees to cover a large share of overhead, so that a gap between developments does not threaten payroll. Suppose you want asset management fees to cover 40 percent of the target, 400,000 dollars a year, and development fees the other 60 percent, 600,000 dollars a year.

Step 2: work back to the stabilised portfolio

Suppose asset management fees average a hypothetical 3 percent of each building's effective gross income, the rent actually collected. To earn 400,000 dollars a year, the buildings must collect 400,000 divided by 0.03, which is about 13,300,000 dollars of rent a year. If a typical building collects 2,000,000 dollars, that is about seven buildings under management. If you own and manage three today, the gap is four. This is the number that tells you holding buildings is not only an investment choice; it is the company's salary.

Say that out loud now.

Recurring fees are the company's salary. The number of buildings I manage decides whether payroll is safe.

Step 3: work back to active developments

Suppose development fees are a hypothetical 3 percent of total project cost, paid evenly over a 36-month development period. A 30,000,000 dollar project produces 900,000 dollars over three years, which is 300,000 dollars a year. To earn 600,000 dollars a year, you need about two projects of that size in development at any time. Because each lasts three years, you must start, on average, two new projects every three years, about one every 18 months, simply to stay level.

Step 4: work back to the pipeline

Now the funnel. Suppose, from your own records, one in five sites you seriously underwrite reaches a signed purchase agreement, and one in two signed purchases reaches construction after approvals and financing. So one in ten underwritten sites becomes a project. To start one project every 18 months, you must underwrite about ten sites every 18 months, or one every seven or eight weeks. And if one in four leads you look at deserves full underwriting, you must screen about 40 leads every 18 months, a little more than two a month. The conversion rates here are invented for arithmetic; measure your own.

Step 5: test the timing gap

The backward calculation assumes a steady state. Reality is lumpy. Suppose one project completes and the next is delayed nine months in approvals. Development fee income falls by 300,000 dollars a year, 25,000 dollars a month, for nine months: 225,000 dollars lost. With asset management fees covering 400,000 of 830,000 dollars of overhead and one development still paying 300,000, the company runs a shortfall of about 130,000 dollars a year until the delayed project starts. Your cash reserve should cover the longest gap you can reasonably foresee. A reserve of six to twelve months of overhead is a common rule of thumb among practitioners, not a standard; the right figure is the one your own gap analysis supports.

A second worked example: what one hire requires

Work one hire backward. A second project manager costs 140,000 dollars a year fully loaded. With a 20 percent margin, he needs about 168,000 dollars of fee income. At 300,000 dollars a year per active development, that is a little more than half a project. So the second project manager makes sense only when the pipeline will reliably sustain a third active project, or when he frees enough founder time to raise the conversion rate. If neither is true, the hire shortens the runway and adds nothing.

A third check: the founder's salary

Look again at the overhead. If the founder's salary is set at zero to make the numbers work, the company is not covering its costs; it is borrowing from the founder. Include a market salary for your own role in the backward calculation. The number of projects that pays for a company with you paid fairly is the true break-even, and it is the number a buyer, a partner or a successor would use.

Putting the backward plan on one page

LineHypothetical target
Annual overhead830,000
Fee income needed, with 20 percent marginabout 1,000,000
Recurring fees400,000, about seven buildings under management
Development fees600,000, two projects active at all times
Start rateone new project about every 18 months
Underwriting rateone site every seven or eight weeks
Screening ratea little more than two leads a month

Read the bottom line first. If you are not screening two leads a month today, the company you want does not yet have the pipeline to pay for it, whatever the projects in hand look like. Review this page every quarter against actual results, and adjust the company to the pipeline, not the pipeline to your hopes.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a company sized to the best year, which then meets an ordinary gap between projects with a payroll it cannot carry. The control is overhead covered by recurring fees with a margin, a reserve sized to the longest foreseeable gap, and a pipeline measured against the start rate the company needs.

The beginner's mistake

Leaving the founder's own salary out of overhead. A company that only works if its founder works for free is not yet a company.

Callback

In Week 74, Remi taught business development: deal sourcing, pipeline, brokers, landowners and relationships. That lesson described the funnel. This one gives it a target: how many leads, how many underwritings and how many starts the company you want actually requires.

Recap

Start from the team and overhead, add a margin, and split the target between recurring and development fees. Work back to buildings under management, active developments and the start rate. Then to the pipeline, using your own conversion rates. Test the gaps, size the reserve, and pay the founder in the model.

Next: Kema on The Room: the first board meeting with an independent director, and the question about what happens without you.
checklist: I start company planning from the team and overhead I need, plus a margin.
I split target fee income between recurring and development fees.
I know how many buildings under management my recurring target requires.
I know the project start rate needed to keep development fees level.
I measure my own conversion rates from lead to underwriting to start.
I size the company reserve to the longest foreseeable gap between projects.
I include a market salary for my own role in overhead.
head: Field checklist
speak: I plan the company backward. In my hypothetical case, five people and their costs make overhead of 830,000 dollars a year, and with a 20 percent margin the company needs about 1,000,000 dollars of fee income. I want recurring asset management fees to cover 400,000 of that. At 3 percent of collected rent, that needs about 13,300,000 dollars of rent, around seven buildings under management. Development fees cover the other 600,000. At 3 percent of a 30,000,000 dollar project over three years, each project pays 300,000 a year, so I need two in development at any time, which means starting one about every 18 months. If one in ten underwritten sites becomes a project, I must underwrite one every seven or eight weeks. Then I test the gaps, size a reserve to the longest foreseeable one, and include a fair salary for myself, because a company that needs a free founder is not yet a company.
terms: Effective gross income — rent and other income actually collected after vacancy, concessions and credit loss.
Start rate — the number of new projects a company must begin per period to keep development fee income level.
Conversion rate — the share of opportunities at one stage of a pipeline that advance to the next.

hostile.q: Your plan needs a new project every 18 months. Your record shows one in the last three years. Why should I believe the plan?
hostile.a: You should believe the record, not the plan, and so do I. The plan shows the start rate the company needs. The record shows the rate I have achieved. The gap is the work. Until the rate improves, the company is sized to recurring fees and one active development, the second project manager is not hired, and the reserve covers twelve months. I will report the conversion rates each quarter, so we can both see whether the gap is closing.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: The First Board Meeting With an Independent Director
summary: A realistic scene: the company's first meeting with an independent director, who asks what happens if the founder is not there. Learn what to say, what never to say, the question behind the question, when to stay silent and how to hold your state. A monthly thread asks what enough means to you.
body:
An independent director is not there to approve you; she is there to make the company safe without you. The first meeting goes well when you welcome the hard questions instead of defending against them.

Recall

Q. What does a delegation of authority do?

A. It sets in writing who may approve each type of decision, up to what limit, and who must be told, so decisions neither wait for the founder nor happen without anyone.

Q. How do you resolve a sale disagreement with a partner who holds 80 percent?

A. Ask what selling does for them that holding does not, show the after-tax comparison, and offer a structure in between, such as a partial buyout.

Q. What is a factory acceptance test?

A. A test of equipment at the manufacturer's premises, before shipping, to confirm it meets the specification, so that defects are found where they are cheapest to fix.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, the first time you invite an independent person onto your board is the first time someone with real authority can tell you no. Founders often bring their most impressive story to that meeting. The independent director is listening for something else: whether the company can survive its founder's absence, error or overconfidence. This scene is practice for that conversation.

The scene

A hypothetical development company with three buildings under management, one project in construction and one in approvals. The board is you, a fellow shareholder and a new independent director, a retired finance executive. The agenda: approve the delegation of authority, review the company's runway and adopt a conflicts policy. Twenty minutes in, she asks: "If you were in hospital for three months starting tomorrow, what would happen to the project in construction?"

The question behind the question

She is not asking about your health. She is asking three things. Does anyone else know enough to run it? Does anyone else have the authority to sign? And do you know the honest answer, or will you reassure her? Answer all three.

The lines to say

"Honestly, today it would slow down badly, and I want to show you why and what I am doing about it." Then the specifics: "Our project manager runs the site and the contractor relationship. Our controller prepares draws. But only I can sign draw certificates and change orders above 25,000 dollars. The delegation on today's agenda gives the controller and project manager joint authority up to the approved budget, with you countersigning above that. My powers of attorney are in place. What is not in place is anyone who knows the lender as well as I do, and I want your help with that."

Then invite the next question: "What else would you want in place before you would be comfortable?"

Say that out loud now.

Here is the honest answer, here is what I am fixing, and what else would you want in place?

The lines never to say

"That won't happen." It tells her you have not thought about it. "Everything is in my head, but I am very organised." That is precisely the risk she was appointed to reduce. "We are too small for that kind of process." Small companies are the ones a single absence can stop. And never answer a governance question with a growth story; it signals that you hear oversight as an obstacle.

When to stay silent

After you have given the honest answer and asked what else she would want, stop. Let her think and speak. Her first suggestion may be the most valuable sentence in the meeting. When she disagrees with you, do not interrupt; take a note, and respond only after she has finished.

Holding your state

Being questioned in your own company can feel like being judged. Reframe it before the meeting: the questions are the service you appointed her to provide. If you notice defensiveness, a tighter voice or faster speech, slow down and lower your voice slightly. Before the meeting, seated and never while driving, a few slow breaths with a longer out-breath is a practitioner habit some people find steadying; check that with your doctor if you have any condition that makes it unsuitable.

A worked example of the conflicts policy

Later in the meeting, she asks how you will handle the fact that you personally own a site the company may develop. Answer with process, not reassurance: "Under the policy you are approving today, I disclose my interest in writing, two independent appraisals are commissioned, I leave the room, and you and the other director decide. In the hypothetical case of appraisals at 3,600,000 and 3,800,000 dollars, the price could not exceed 3,700,000 without a written reason in the minutes." That one example tells her you understand the rule and intend to live under it.

What she writes after the meeting

Picture her notes. Delegation approved, with countersignature above budget. Key-person gap named honestly: the lender relationship sits with the founder alone. Conflicts policy adopted, with an example the founder volunteered. Runway reported at a stated number of months. Action: introduce a second person to the lender within the quarter. If her notes read like that, the meeting went well, even though you admitted a weakness, and largely because you did.

Follow up within two working days with the minutes in draft, the action list with owners and dates, and the board pack for the next meeting scheduled. An independent director judges a company as much by what arrives after a meeting as by what is said in it.

Family, legacy and what enough means

A monthly thread. The independent director's question, what happens if you are not there, has a personal twin that no board can answer for you. If the company works without you, what do you want your time to be for? Building a company that runs on its own creates a choice most founders never get: to keep growing it, to step back, or to hand it on.

So the question is yours to answer, not ours. What would enough look like for you, in money, in time and in what you leave behind? Write your own answer in a sentence or two, date it, and read it again in a year. Notice whether the company you are building is moving toward that answer or away from it.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is treating the independent director as an audience to impress, so that the company gains a name on its letterhead but no real check. The control is to bring her the hardest questions first, give honest answers, and give her written authority, such as countersignature limits and conflict decisions, that makes her oversight real.

The beginner's mistake

Reassuring instead of answering. "That won't happen" ends the conversation and begins her doubt.

The second mistake is agreeing to every suggestion on the spot to show openness. An independent director respects a founder who says, "I will consider that and bring a recommendation to the next meeting," because it shows the suggestion will be thought through rather than merely accepted. Write each suggestion down, give it an owner and a date, and report on all of them at the next meeting, including the ones you decided against and why.

Callback

In Week 5, Kema taught bottom line first and the pyramid principle. In the boardroom, the bottom line is often an uncomfortable one: "today it would slow down badly." Saying it first, then supporting it, is what earns the independent director's trust in everything you say after it.

Recap

The independent director tests whether the company survives without its founder. Give the honest answer first, show what you are fixing, and ask what else she would want. Never reassure in place of answering. Stay silent while she thinks. Explain conflicts through process with a worked example.

Next: Kema on the week's quiz and recap, with Cole's Auditor's Chair on a set of board minutes.
checklist: I bring the hardest governance questions to the board myself, before I am asked.
I answer key-person questions honestly, starting with the current weakness.
I ask the independent director what else she would want in place.
I never answer a governance question with a growth story.
I give the independent director real authority, such as countersignature and conflict decisions.
I explain conflicts through the written process, with an example.
I have written my own answer to what enough means, and dated it.
head: Field checklist
speak: At the first meeting with an independent director, she will ask what happens if I am not there. Behind that question are three: does anyone else know enough to run it, does anyone else have authority to sign, and do I know the honest answer? So I start with the truth: today it would slow down badly. Then the specifics: who runs the site, who prepares draws, who can sign now, and how the delegation on the agenda changes that, with her countersigning above the budget. Then I name what is still missing, and ask what else she would want in place. I never say it won't happen, never claim it is all organised in my head, and never answer oversight with a growth story. On conflicts, I explain the process with an example. And I remember the personal twin of her question, which only I can answer: what would enough look like for me?
terms: Countersignature — a second authorised signature required on a document or payment above a set limit.
Conflicts policy — a written board procedure for disclosing and deciding transactions in which a director or owner has a personal interest.
Board pack — the papers circulated to directors before a meeting, so decisions are made on information.

hostile.q: You hold most of the votes. If I disagree with you on a conflict, what stops you overruling me?
hostile.a: The conflicts policy we adopt today, and the shareholders' agreement amendment that goes with it. Any transaction in which I have an interest needs your approval, and I do not vote on it. If I tried to overrule you, I would be acting outside the policy and in breach of my own duties, and you would have the minutes to show it. I want that check to be real, which is why I asked you to join.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 128 Review: The Company as a System, and Cole's Auditor's Chair
summary: Six questions test the week's ideas on building the company. Because this is a fourth week, Cole takes the Auditor's Chair to read hypothetical board minutes as a hostile auditor would. A two-minute boardroom drill closes the week.
body:
This week came down to one test: would the company keep making good, honest decisions if you were absent tomorrow, and could anyone prove from the records that it had?

Recall

Q. What should a founder say first when an independent director asks what would happen in his absence?

A. The honest answer, including the current weakness, then what is being fixed, then a question about what else she would want in place.

Q. What is the trap of debt above tax cost?

A. After repeated cash-out refinances, a sale can produce more tax on the gain than the cash left after repaying the loan.

Q. What does a cap rate effect describe?

A. The part of a change in value caused by the cap rate moving rather than by a change in NOI.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, a company is the only asset you build that can outlast your attention. Answer each question aloud before reading the answer.

The six questions

Question 1. What are the three layers of governance, and what does each decide?

Answer: Owners appoint the board and decide structural matters. The board sets strategy, approves major commitments and oversees management. Management runs the business within limits the board sets.

Question 2. What four controls reduce key-person risk?

Answer: Documented processes, named deputies for each critical role, insurance concepts assessed by a licensed adviser, and legal arrangements such as powers of attorney and a shareholders' agreement covering incapacity.

Question 3. What is Cole's related-party test?

Answer: Written disclosure to everyone affected, approval by someone with no interest, and price evidence from an independent source.

Question 4. Why should steady fees cover steady costs?

Answer: Because payroll arrives every two weeks and the promote arrives years later, if at all. Funding overhead from an expected promote pushes founders into poor deals or into project accounts.

Question 5. What makes a buy-sell clause work?

Answer: A clear trigger, a valuation method and a funding source, reviewed as the company's value changes.

Question 6. State Rule 128.

Answer: Never transact with your own company without written disclosure, independent approval and independent price evidence; the more control you hold, the stronger the check you must build on yourself.

Say that out loud now.

Recap of the week

Omar and Kema framed the company as a system that works without its founder: governance, delegation, key-person risk, hiring order, systems and brand. Ford and Cole took WeWork in 2019, governance built around one person, giving Rule 128. Nadia priced overhead against fees and runway. Omar taught directors' duties, conflicts and the shareholders' agreement. Nadia reverse engineered how many projects pay for the team. Kema ran the first meeting with an independent director.

Cole's Auditor's Chair

Week 128 is a fourth week, so the Red Pen becomes Cole's Auditor's Chair: read these hypothetical board minutes as a hostile auditor would. Find the defects before reading on.

Minutes of the Board, held by telephone. Present: the Chief Executive (chair) and one other director. The Chief Executive reported that the company will acquire a site from Founder Holdings for 4,000,000 dollars, a fair price in his view. Approved. The Chief Executive will also receive a development fee on the project at a rate to be agreed later. Approved. The company's monthly overhead of 60,000 dollars will be funded from the project account until the promote is received. Approved. The Chief Executive confirmed that all directors are independent.

The defects. First, the Chief Executive almost certainly has an interest in Founder Holdings, yet there is no written disclosure, no abstention and no record that the other director decided without him. Second, the price rests on "his view", with no appraisal or other independent evidence. Third, a fee "at a rate to be agreed later" is an approval of nothing, and it is another related-party payment with no process. Fourth, funding company overhead from the project account is likely a breach of the project documents and mixes company and project money. Fifth, relying on the promote to repay it treats an uncertain reward as income. Sixth, a director with a direct interest cannot confirm that all directors are independent, and with two directors present, one of them conflicted, there may be no valid quorum for the conflicted items; check the constitution. An auditor would also note that the minutes record no papers circulated and no reasons, which leaves the directors poorly protected on the duty of care.

The boardroom drill

Stand up and explain this week in two minutes. Then compare with the model answer.

Model answer: "Our company is designed to work without me. Owners appoint the board, the board approves major commitments and oversees management, and a written delegation of authority sets who can approve what, matched to our bank mandates. We reduce key-person risk with documented processes, named deputies, insurance concepts and a shareholders' agreement that covers death, disability and departure, with a funded buy-sell. Steady fees cover steady costs, and we report the company's runway monthly. Every hire has a fee-based business case. Any transaction with me or my affiliates is disclosed in writing, priced on independent evidence and approved by someone without an interest, because the more control I hold, the stronger the check must be."

Score yourself: bottom line first, the three governance layers, the four key-person controls, Rule 128, under two minutes.

How to use this review

Mark any answer you gave slowly or vaguely, return to that day's lesson and read only the section that answers it, and answer again tomorrow, aloud. This week, Question 2 and Question 6 matter most, because they are the ones a lender and an investor will each ask you, in their own words, before they commit.

Then do one practical exercise. Take a blank page and draft your own company's delegation of authority: six decision types down the side, three columns for who approves, the limit and who must be told. It will take twenty minutes. Where you cannot fill a box, you have found a gap in the company, and that gap is this week's real homework. Do the same with a related-party register: list every arrangement between you, your entities and any project, even the harmless ones. A list that seems unnecessary when it has two lines is exactly the list an investor will ask for when it has ten.

Finally, rehearse Cole's chair on paper you wrote yourself. Pick the last set of minutes, approval email or investment memo you produced and read it as someone who wanted to find fault. Ask three questions of every decision in it: who decided, on what evidence, and was anyone deciding about their own interest? The habit is uncomfortable the first few times. After that it becomes how you write, and documents written that way rarely need defending.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk this week is a company whose records cannot show that conflicts were handled and decisions were informed. The control is board papers before decisions, written disclosure of every conflict, abstention, independent evidence and minutes with reasons.

The beginner's mistake

Writing minutes that record outcomes but not reasons. "Approved" protects nobody; "approved because the two appraisals averaged 3,700,000 dollars and the interested director abstained" protects everybody.

Callback

In Week 83, Cole taught audit and critique: independent reviews, red teams and critiquing your own team. This week's Auditor's Chair is that discipline pointed at yourself. The most valuable audit you will ever commission is of your own governance, while it is still small enough to fix.

Recap

A company is a system: governance in three layers, a written delegation, key-person controls, hiring that strengthens controls first, steady fees for steady costs, and conflicts handled by process. Rule 128 builds the check on the person with the most control.

Next: Remi, with Warrick and Marco, on First Principles: how elite developers, contractors and wealth builders structured fees, capital, delivery and growth, reverse engineered from verified facts.
checklist: What are the three layers of governance, and what does each decide?
What four controls reduce key-person risk?
What is Cole's related-party test?
Why should steady fees cover steady costs?
What makes a buy-sell clause work?
State Rule 128.
head: The six questions
speak: This week I learned to build the company as a system that works without me. Owners appoint the board, the board approves major commitments and oversees management, and management runs the business within a written delegation of authority that matches our bank mandates. I reduce key-person risk with documented processes, named deputies, insurance concepts assessed by a licensed adviser, and a shareholders' agreement that covers death, disability and departure, with a funded buy-sell. Project money and company money stay separate. Steady fees cover steady costs, the promote is a reward, the company's runway is reported monthly, and every hire has a fee-based business case. Directors owe loyalty and care, and their protection is a record of informed decisions. Rule 128: never transact with my own company without written disclosure, independent approval and independent price evidence, because the more control I hold, the stronger the check must be.
terms: Auditor's Chair — Cole's drill of reading a document as a hostile auditor would, looking for gaps in process, evidence and authority.
Quorum — the minimum number of eligible directors who must be present for a board decision to be valid, as set by the constitution or law.
Abstention — a conflicted director's withdrawal from discussion and voting on a matter in which he has an interest.

hostile.q: These minutes approve a 4,000,000 dollar purchase from your own holding company on your view of fairness. Why is that not a breach of your duties?
hostile.a: On these minutes, I cannot show it is not, and that is the problem. I will not rely on them. The purchase will come back to the board with my interest disclosed in writing, two independent appraisals, the fee terms fixed, and the decision taken by the other directors without me, with reasons minuted. The overhead item is withdrawn; company costs will be paid from company funds only.
